claim: Estrogen (E2) and Progesterone (Pg), via their specific receptors (ERalpha and PR), are major determinants in the development and progression of endometrial carcinomas.
source: Estrogen (E2) and Progesterone (Pg), via their specific receptors (ERalpha and PR), are major determinants in the development and progression of endometrial carcinomas
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field of endometrial cancer research.

claim: E2 treatment exposes a set of progestin-dependent PR binding sites which include both E2 and progestin target genes in Ishikawa endometrial cancer cells.
source: Using Ishikawa endometrial cancer cells, we report that E2 treatment exposes a set of progestin-dependent PR binding sites which include both E2 and progestin target genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript showing PR binding sites after E2 pretreatment.

claim: ChIP-seq results from hormone-treated cells revealed a non-random distribution of PAX2 binding in the vicinity of estrogen-promoted PR sites.
source: ChIP-seq results from hormone-treated cells revealed a non-random distribution of PAX2 binding in the vicinity of these estrogen-promoted PR sites.
evidence: This is directly supported by ChIP-seq experimental data showing PAX2 binding patterns near PR sites.

claim: Altered expression of hormone regulated genes in PAX2 knockdown cells suggests a role for PAX2 in fine-tuning ERalpha and PR interplay in transcriptional regulation.
source: Altered expression of hormone regulated genes in PAX2 knockdown cells suggests a role for PAX2 in fine-tuning ERalpha and PR interplay in transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from PAX2 knockdown experiments and gene expression analysis.

claim: Progestin control regions (PgCRs) exhibited an open chromatin state even before hormone exposure.
source: Analysis of long-range interactions by Hi-C coupled with ATAC-seq data showed that these regions, that we call 'progestin control regions' (PgCRs), exhibited an open chromatin state even before hormone exposure
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data showing chromatin accessibility at PgCRs in untreated cells.

claim: PgCRs were non-randomly associated with regulated genes.
source: Analysis of long-range interactions by Hi-C coupled with ATAC-seq data showed that these regions, that we call 'progestin control regions' (PgCRs), exhibited an open chromatin state even before hormone exposure and were non-randomly associated with regulated genes.
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data showing interactions between PgCRs and gene promoters.

claim: Nearly 20% of genes potentially influenced by PgCRs were found to be altered during progression of endometrial cancer.
source: Nearly 20% of genes potentially influenced by PgCRs were found to be altered during progression of endometrial cancer.
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA endometrial cancer data comparing genes in TADs with PgCRs to differentially expressed genes across cancer stages.

claim: Progesterone (Pg) is a key regulator in the female reproductive tract, including uterine and mammary gland development (Lydon et al., 1995).
source: Progesterone (Pg) is a key regulator in the female reproductive tract, including uterine and mammary gland development (Lydon et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: During pregnancy, Pg prepares the uterine epithelium to receive the embryo and initiates the process of differentiation of stromal cells toward their decidual phenotype.
source: During pregnancy, Pg prepares the uterine epithelium to receive the embryo and initiates the process of differentiation of stromal cells toward their decidual phenotype.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about progesterone function in pregnancy.

claim: In the mammary gland and in coordination with prolactin, Pg stimulates epithelial proliferation and differentiation of alveolar lobes in the mammary gland (Mulac-Jericevic and Conneely, 2004).
source: In the mammary gland and in coordination with prolactin, Pg stimulates epithelial proliferation and differentiation of alveolar lobes in the mammary gland (Mulac-Jericevic and Conneely, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Estradiol (E2) is the main proliferative signal in the uterine epithelium and exerts its function through activating estrogen receptor (ER) alpha and beta (ERalpha and beta, respectively) (Ishiwata et al., 1997; Kayisli et al., 2004).
source: Unlike Pg, estradiol (E2) is the main proliferative signal in the uterine epithelium and exerts its function through activating estrogen receptor (ER) alpha and beta (ERalpha and beta, respectively) (Ishiwata et al., 1997; Kayisli et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The physiological role of Pg is mediated by the interaction and consequent activation of isoforms A (PRA) and B (PRB) of the progesterone receptor (PR), which are transcribed from alternate promoters of the gene (Hovland et al., 1998).
source: The physiological role of Pg is mediated by the interaction and consequent activation of isoforms A (PRA) and B (PRB) of the progesterone receptor (PR), which are transcribed from alternate promoters of the gene (Hovland et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PRA is more abundant in stromal endometrial cells.
source: While PRA is more abundant in stromal endometrial cells, PRB is the most representative isoform in ephitelial cells of endometrium.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about PR isoform distribution in endometrial tissue.

claim: PRB is the most representative isoform in epithelial cells of endometrium.
source: While PRA is more abundant in stromal endometrial cells, PRB is the most representative isoform in ephitelial cells of endometrium.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about PR isoform distribution in endometrial tissue.

claim: Estradiol exposure triggers ER binding to estrogen response elements (ERE) regulating target genes such as PGR.
source: Estradiol exposure triggers ER binding to estrogen response elements (ERE) regulating target genes such as PGR.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about estrogen receptor mechanism of action.

claim: Previous work showed E2-dependent upregulation of PR in many different target cells, species and pathological conditions (Graham et al., 1995; Kraus and Katzenellenbogen, 1993).
source: Previous work showed E2-dependent upregulation of PR in many different target cells, species and pathological conditions (Graham et al., 1995; Kraus and Katzenellenbogen, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: High levels of PRA and PRB have been described in endometrial hyperplasia (Miyamoto et al., 2004).
source: High levels of PRA and PRB have been described in endometrial hyperplasia (Miyamoto et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Low- and high-grade endometrial cancers reveal reduced or absent expression of one or both PR isoforms in epithelia or stroma (Shao, 2013).
source: while low- and high-grade endometrial cancers reveal reduced or absent expression of one or both isoforms in epithelia or stroma (Shao, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PR decrease is often associated with shorter progression-free survival and overall survival rates (Leslie et al., 1997; Miyamoto et al., 2004; Sakaguchi et al., 2004; Jongen et al., 2009; Kreizman-Shefer et al., 2014).
source: This PR decrease is often associated with shorter progression-free survival and overal survival rates (Leslie et al., 1997; Miyamoto et al., 2004; Sakaguchi et al., 2004; Jongen et al., 2009; Kreizman-Shefer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: ER but not PR was directly involved in the proliferative response to E2 in Ishikawa cells.
source: proving that ER but not PR was directly involved in the proliferative response to E2.
evidence: This is inferred from the antagonist experiments showing ICI182780 but not RU486 blocks E2-induced proliferation.

claim: Suppression of E2-induced cell proliferation by R5020 was inhibited by pre-incubation with RU486 (FC 1.50±0.06 v. OH), indicating that R5020 effect was mediated by PR in Ishikawa cells.
source: Suppression of E2-induced cell proliferation by R5020 was inhibited by pre-incubation with RU486 (FC 1.50±0.06 v. OH), indicating that R5020 effect was mediated by PR in Ishikawa cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The percentage of cells exhibiting nuclear localization of PR increased upon E2 pretreatment prior to R5020 exposure.
source: The percentage of cells exhibiting nuclear localization of PR increased upon E2 pretreatment prior to R5020 exposure (T0).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Upon exposure to R5020 for 60 min the percentage of cells exhibiting nuclear PR was not affected by E2 pretreatment, though the intensity of the fluorescence signal increased in E2-pretreated cells.
source: Upon exposure to R5020 for 60 min the percentage of cells exhibiting nuclear PR was not affected by E2 pretreatment, though the intensity of the fluorescence signal increased in E2-pretreated cells
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ishikawa cells express considerably higher levels of ERalpha than of ERbeta.
source: Ishikawa cells express considerably higher levels of ERalpha than of ERbeta
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: R5020 increased nuclear ERalpha, suggesting a functional PR-ER crosstalk in response to hormonal stimuli.
source: R5020 increased nuclear ERalpha, suggesting a functional PR-ER crosstalk in response to hormonal stimuli
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: A 2.8 fold increment in Luciferase activity was found in cells exposed to R5020 relative to OH controls, supporting the capacity of ligand-activated PR to activate PREs.
source: A 2.8 fold increment in Luciferase activity was found in cells exposed to R5020 relative to OH controls, supporting the capacity of ligand-activated PR to activate PREs
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PR ChIPseq showed robust PR binding after 30 min of R5020 treatment with 1,446 sites, of which 322 sites (22%) were present in untreated cells.
source: Results showed robust PR binding after 30 min of R5020 treatment (R5020 30 min) with 1,446 sites, of which 322 sites (22%) were present in untreated cells (PRbs at time zero, T0 = 331).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: After 60 min of treatment with R5020, the majority of sites identified at 30 min were still evident (78%).
source: After 60 min of treatment with R5020 (R5020 60 min), the majority of sites identified at 30 min were still evident (78%)
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Exposure to E2 resulted in the detection of 178 ERalpha binding sites (ERbs) at 5 min, 1591 at 60 min and 1,973 at 360 min.
source: Exposure to E2 resulted in the detection of 178 ERalpha binding sites (ERbs) at 5 min, 1591 at 60 min and 1,973 at 360 min
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The majority (85%) of ERbs found at 60 min was also identified at 360 min.
source: The majority (85%) of ERbs found at 60 min was also identified at 360 min
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: De novo motif discovery confirmed that PR binding occurred mostly through PREs exhibiting the complete palindromic response elements.
source: De novo motif discovery confirmed that PR binding occurred mostly through PREs exhibiting the complete palindromic response elements
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: ER binding sites were enriched in half-palindromic ERE motifs.
source: while ER binding sites were enriched in half-palindromic ERE motifs
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Pretreatment with E2 significantly increased the number of R5020-dependent PRbs (prePRbs), which included most of PRbs already identified in non-pretreated Ishikawa cells.
source: Pretreatment with E2 significantly increased the number of R5020-dependent PRbs (prePRbs), which included most of PRbs already identified in non-pretreated Ishikawa cells
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The number of PRbs doubled between 30 and 60 min of R5020 in preE2 cells, reaching 5701 sites.
source: Contrary to PRbs in non-pretreated cells, the number of PRbs doubled between 30 and 60 min of R5020 in preE2 cells, reaching 5701 sites
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The majority of PRbs identified in Ishikawa cells (>90%) were also detected in FPR cells.
source: The majority of PRbs identified in Ishikawa cells ( > 90%) were also detected in FPR cells
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Nearly 50% of binding sites localized to distal regions (>50 Kb) and approximately 30% to introns other than the first intron.
source: Nearly 50% of binding sites localized to distal regions ( > 50 Kb) and approximately 30% to introns other than the first intron
evidence: This is supported by genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Of the 1886 genes regulated by R5020, only 224 (12%) were potentially associated to PRbs.
source: Of the 1886 genes regulated by R5020, only 224 (12%) were potentially associated to PRbs
evidence: This is supported by GREAT analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only 199 of the 950 genes regulated by E2 (21%) proved to be associated to ERbs.
source: while only 199 of the 950 genes regulated by E2 (21%) proved to be associated to ERbs
evidence: This is supported by GREAT analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Enrichment of multiple members of the PAX family -including variants 2, 5, 6, and 9- was found in Ishikawa-specific PRbs and ERbs.
source: Results revealed an enrichment (p-value < 1 e-4) of multiple members of the PAX family -including variants 2, 5, 6, and 9- in groups I and III, that is In Ishikawa-specific PRbs and ERbs
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Stronger enrichment of PAX motifs was observed in prePRbs compared to PRbs.
source: Stronger enrichment of PAX motifs was observed in prePRbs compared to PRbs
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PAX2 and the ubiquitous AP1 were the only TFs predicted to bind both E2 and R5020-regulated genes.
source: PAX2 and the ubiquitous AP1 were the only TFs (including other PAX family members) predicted to bind both E2 and R5020-regulated genes.
evidence: This is supported by DAVID analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of PAX2 was significantly reduced in tumor samples (Endometrioid and Serous adenocarcinomas) compared to normal tissue.
source: in which expression of PAX2 was significantly reduced in tumor samples (Endometrioid and Serous adenocarcinomas) compared to normal tissue
evidence: This is supported by analysis of publicly available RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nuclear localization of PAX2 was observed predominantly after 60 min of R5020 in pretreated and non-pretreated PR+ cells.
source: Nuclear localization of PAX2 was observed predominantly after 60 min of R5020 in pretreated and non-pretreated PR+ cells
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PAX2 binding was not stochastically distributed in the genome of Ishikawa cells but rather partially associated to ERbs and PRbs.
source: Moreover, PAX2 binding was not stochastically distributed in the genome of Ishikawa cells but rather partially associated to ERbs and PRbs
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data and overlap analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The association between PAX2 and binding of the receptors was statistically significant (two-tailed Fisher's exact test; p-value < 0.001).
source: In agreement with the coverage plots, the association between PAX2 and binding of the receptors was statistically significant (two-tailed Fisher's exact test; p-value < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ChIP-seq overlap shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Knock down of PAX2 under estrogenic conditions led to a significant R5020-dependent increased binding of PR to regulatory regions upstream of TGFA and in TIPARP promoter.
source: Interestingly, knock down of PAX2 under estrogenic conditions led to a significant R5020-dependent increased binding of PR to regulatory regions upstream of TGFA and in TIPARP promoter
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data after PAX2 knockdown shown in Figure 5H.

claim: In the absence of E2 pretreatment, R5020-dependent expression of ALPP was abolished by PAX2 knock down, while TIPARP regulation was practically unaffected.
source: In the absence of E2 pretreatment, R5020-dependent expression of ALPP was abolished by PAX2 knock down, while TIPARP regulation was practically unaffected
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data after PAX2 knockdown shown in Figure 5I.

claim: A comparison of contact matrices at 20 kb resolution of untreated Ishikawa cells to T47D cells confirmed the high degree of conservation on the borders of topologically associating domains (TADs).
source: A comparison of contact matrices at 20 kb resolution of untreated Ishikawa cells to T47D cells confirmed the high degree of conservation on the borders of topologically associating domains (TADs)
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A/B profile distribution in Ishikawa cells was independent from hormonal treatments.
source: However, A/B profile distribution in Ishikawa cells was independent from hormonal treatments
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C compartment analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and E.

claim: 7% of A domains in Ishikawa cells were B in T47D cells, and 12% of B domains in Ishikawa cells were A in T47D cells.
source: Detailed analysis revealed that 7% of A domains in Ishikawa cells were B in T47D cells, and 12% of B domains in Ishikawa cells were A in T47D cells
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C compartment comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Both transcription factors, PR and ER alpha, bound A compartments more frequently than B.
source: Both transcription factors, PR and ER alpha, bound A compartments more frequently than B
evidence: This is supported by analysis of ChIP-seq data relative to Hi-C compartments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: 121 PgCRs were identified in Ishikawa cells.
source: In agreement with this restriction, the sizes of PgCR -with an average of 25kb- were smaller than TADs -with an average of 1000kb- (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I). In addition, the majority of the 121 identified PgCRs (coordinates in hg38 Figure 6—source data 2) were not located near the TAD borders, but in the TAD center
evidence: This is based on computational analysis defining PgCRs according to specific criteria.

claim: ATACseq signal on PgCRs remained unchanged upon hormone exposure.
source: Consistent with these results, ATACseq signal on PgCRs remained unchanged upon hormone exposure
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both R5020- and E2-regulated genes with highest FC values were concentrated under 1 Mb away from PgCRs.
source: In addition, both R5020- and E2-regulated genes with highest FC values (v. T0) were concentrated under 1 Mb ('close') away from PgCRs
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PgCRs preferentially interact with promoters of hormone-regulated genes.
source: Further analysis on Hi-C contact matrices revealed that PgCRs preferentially interact with promoters of hormone-regulated genes
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C interaction analysis shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: PgCR-promoter interactions were non-random and mostly intra-TAD.
source: Although PgCR-promoter interactions were non-random and mostly intra-TAD, we found no difference in contact enrichment between treated and untreated cells
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C interaction analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: No difference in contact enrichment between treated and untreated cells was found for PgCR-promoter interactions.
source: Although PgCR-promoter interactions were non-random and mostly intra-TAD, we found no difference in contact enrichment between treated and untreated cells
evidence: This is supported by Hi-C interaction analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 102 genes were located in TADs with PgCRs and were also differentially expressed in Stage IV endometrial cancer.
source: Among these differentially expressed genes (DEGs), we found that 102 genes (Figure 7—source data 1) were also located in TADs with PgCRs including both upregulated and downregulated genes
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: These 102 genes constitute 20% of the 522 protein coding genes in TADs with PgCRs.
source: These 102 genes constitute 20% of the 522 protein coding genes in TADs with PgCRs (PgCR-genes; Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the intersection of differentially expressed genes and genes in TADs with PgCRs.

claim: The 102 intersected genes were not part of the normal distribution generated by random sampling, as demonstrated by bootstrapping analysis.
source: Each intersection was then used to build a distribution (µ71.58) and a 95% confidence interval (2.5%=57; 97.5%=87) that demonstrated that the 102 intersected genes were in fact not part of the normal distribution
evidence: This is supported by bootstrapping statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Genes downregulated in tumor progression were mostly clustered together among genes upregulated by E2 (NES = 1.25; FDR = 0.1669) or R5020 (NES = 0.99; FDR = 0.9547) in Ishikawa cells.
source: Although GSEA results were not statistically robust, genes downregulated in tumor progression were mostly clustered together among genes upregulated by E2 (NES = 1.25; FDR = 0.1669) or R5020 (NES = 0.99; FDR = 0.9547) in Ishikawa cells.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: In Ishikawa cells, binding of ER and PR occurs mainly at ERE and PRE sequences, respectively, in regions that are also enriched in PAX response elements.
source: In Ishikawa cells, binding of ER and PR occurs mainly at ERE and PRE sequences, respectively, in regions that are also enriched in PAX response elements.
evidence: This is based on motif analysis of ChIP-seq data showing enrichment of these motifs.

claim: In Ishikawa cells, PR binding has little influence on ERalpha binding, contrary to what was described in breast cancer cells.
source: This indicates that contrary to what was described in breast cancer cells (Mohammed et al., 2015; Singhal et al., 2016), in endometrial cells PR binding has little influence on ERalpha binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the limited overlap between PR and ER binding sites in Ishikawa cells compared to previous reports in breast cancer cells.

claim: PRbs and ERbs are enriched in Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) containing hormone-regulated genes.
source: When we analyzed chromatin topology of Ishikawa cells using Hi-C we found that PRbs and ERbs are enriched in Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) containing hormone-regulated genes.
evidence: This is based on integration of ChIP-seq and Hi-C data.

claim: These TADs were predominantly part of the open (A) chromosome compartment, even in cells not exposed to hormone.
source: These TADs were predominantly part of the open (A) chromosome compartment, even in cells not exposed to hormone.
evidence: This is based on Hi-C compartment analysis.

claim: The sites where the hormone receptors will bind were already accessible, suggesting that hormone-independent mechanisms were responsible for the generation and maintenance of the hormone-responsive TADs.
source: This was confirmed by ATACseq results showing that the sites where the hormone receptors will bind were already accessible, suggesting that hormone-independent mechanisms were responsible for the generation and maintenance of the hormone-responsive TADs.
evidence: This is inferred from ATAC-seq data showing open chromatin at receptor binding sites before hormone treatment.

claim: PAX2 could generate the open chromatin conformation that enables PR binding and facilitates the interacting loops detected in Hi-C experiments.
source: In that respect, it is interesting that we found an enrichment of PAXbs near PRbs in these TADs containing progesterone regulated genes, suggesting that PAX2 could generate the open chromatin conformation that enables PR binding and facilitates the interacting loops detected in Hi-C experiments.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the enrichment of PAX2 binding near PR sites and the open chromatin state.

claim: Loss of PAX2 expression has been implicated in the development of endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN) (Sanderson et al., 2017).
source: Loss of PAX2 expression has been implicated in the development of endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN) (Sanderson et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PAX2 is potentially useful in the diagnostic of difficult EIN cases (Quick et al., 2012).
source: and PAX2 is potentially useful in the diagnostic of difficult EIN cases (e.g. where there is no 'normal' tissue available to act as an internal control when assessing nuclear morphology) (Quick et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: E2-induced ERalpha acts together with PAX2 to define key PR regulatory regions that modulate gene expression.
source: In line with this notion, we propose that E2-induced ERalpha acts together with PAX2 to define key PR regulatory regions that modulate gene expression.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings showing enrichment of PAX2 near ER and PR binding sites.

claim: PR-PAX-PR binding sites containing regulatory domains (PgCRs) could reflect PR shadow enhancers in endometrial cells.
source: We hypothesize that PR-PAX-PR binding sites containing regulatory domains that we name PgCRs could reflect PR shadow enhancers (Cannavò et al., 2016) in endometrial cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the characteristics of PgCRs and comparison to shadow enhancers described in other systems.

claim: Combinations of the same hormone receptors and different transcription factors account for cell-type-specific expression of different gene regulatory networks in part by generating and maintaining different genome topologies.
source: Thus, combinations of the same hormone receptors and different transcription factors account for cell-type-specific expression of different gene regulatory networks in part by generating and maintaining different genome topologies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of Ishikawa and T47D cells showing different partner TFs (PAX2 vs FOXA1) and different chromatin topologies.

claim: Loss of PAX2 forces aberrant PR and ER alpha signaling in endometrial cells that may lead to the altered expression of both receptors and consequently PgCR-genes, facilitating the progression of the disease.
source: In conclusion, it is our belief that loss of PAX2 forces aberrant PR and ER alpha signaling in endometrial cells that may lead to the altered expression of both receptors and consequently PgCR-genes, facilitating the progression of the disease.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed reduction of PAX2 in cancer samples and the effects of PAX2 knockdown on gene expression.
